newsitem.title: UK: Investors recover equanimity after Lebed sacking.
newsitem.headline: Investors recover equanimity after Lebed sacking.

text.p: Investors recovered equanimity on Friday following Thursday's surprise sacking of Russian security chief Alexander Lebed, which highlighted political tension in Moscow and put the current fragile peace in Chechnia at risk. Russian debt prices quickly recovered most of the ground they initially lost on Thursday in London trading.
Following are some comments from investors:
MICHAEL JORDAN, VICE PRESIDENT OF EMERGING MARKETS, BANKAMERICA
"I don't think we're going to see (debt) prices skyrocket at the moment.
There was always going to be a correction, no matter what, and it was just a bit deeper than expected, but prices will ratchet back up."
"I wouldn't expect these events to delay the Eurobond, in fact it smooths the passage, because it takes away the (mud) slinging within the government."
"Our clients are quite comfortable with what's happened."
JEROME BOOTH, HEAD OF EMERGING MARKETS RESEARCH, ANZ GRINDLAYS
"The implications for Chechnya, now the deal is done, are less than during the period of negotiation. But it is not good news for Chechnya, it's certainly a negative."
"For economic policy and sovereign risk, it's certainly on the good side."
"In the ratings this was taken into account. Russia in one to two years will be investment grade. We see a situation in Russia where all the risks are short term."
RICHARD SEGAL, SANTANDER INVESTMENT, NEW YORK

"Vnesh loans plunged to pre-rating levels, meaning that the rating agency warnings about the possibility of "future tensions" have come to the front more quickly than expected. As a result, the rating agency that unveiled the more cautious guidelines appears to have won the first round."
"It has become clear that President Yeltsin is fully involved in in the process of government; speculation about his withdrawal has now been forgotten."
"It was speculated earlier this week that Mr Lebed may form a coalition with the President's former bodyguard Alexander Korzhakov. This bloc will now have a freer rein to coalesce."
"It is difficult to find implications for economic policy; thus the events are neutral, at worst, for Russia's sovereign debt." --Caroline Brothers, London Newsroom +44 171 542 2734
